b: Each sequel to Meet the Parents has found new, awkward ways to put Ben Stiller’s Greg Focker through a gauntlet of humiliations like the one he endured in Jay Roach’s 2000 comedy. Where 2004’s Meet the Fockers introduced Greg’s hippie parents, 2010’s Little Fockers found him and his wife, Pam (Teri Polo), raising twins. Yet both films, like the original, made Greg’s ever-deepening anxiety and paranoia around his father-in-law, Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro), their chief source of comic hijinks.

Now, 16 years after the third installment of this unlikely, and wholly unnecessary, franchise, John Hamburg’s Focker In-Law catches up with the Focker family just as Greg’s son, Henry (Skyler Gisondo), is preparing to propose to his girlfriend, Olivia (Ariana Grande). For a time, this setup shifts the film’s tension away from Greg and the domineering Jack and toward Greg and Olivia, a former FBI hostage negotiator whose professional skills lead the overprotective Greg to suspect that she’s manipulating his son and trying to pull him away from his parents.

As the meddling future father-in-law, Greg is primed for a role reversal, his suspicions of Olivia putting him in the alpha position typically reserved for Jack. In scenes where Greg and Olivia engage in psychological warfare, or where Greg navigates his changing relationship with Henry, Focker In-Law at least brings something fresh to the table. But outside of those few moments, the film reverts to the same jokes and narrative beats as the three films that came before it.

Dutifully and belaboredly replaying the hits, Focker In-Law, which Hamburg scripted from a story he co-wrote with Ilana Glazer and Austen Earl, serves up yet another polygraph scene, gives Greg another run-in with Jack’s now-taxidermied cat, Mr. Jinx, and brings back Pam’s ex-fiancé, Kevin (Owen Wilson), to once again serve as a foil to Greg’s fragile ego. Most groan-worthy of all, though, are the continued jokes about Greg’s birth name, Gaylord, and an excruciatingly extended bit with a snobby flight attendant who won’t let him use the first-class bathroom—a gag that would’ve felt stale even in Roach’s original film.

It also doesn’t help that, aside from Grande, the film’s women are little more than window dressing. Pam is there primarily to comfort Greg after his mishaps; their daughter, Samantha (Beanie Feldstein), plays second fiddle to her loopy, seemingly stoned longtime boyfriend, Eduardo (Eduardo Franco), who longs to be welcomed into Jack’s “circle of trust”; and Pam’s mother, Dina (Blythe Danner), barely gets a word in edgewise.

There’s an amusing scene in Focker In-Law in which Greg is forced, for reasons that actually make sense, to serenade Jack with John Legend’s “All of Me,” and it finds De Niro flexing his deadpan comedy chops. Unfortunately, little else in Hamburg’s film generates even a chuckle. So much of Focker In-Law plays like warmed-over leftovers from the earlier entries in a series that, after its last two installments, should’ve been allowed to die a dignified death.

Score:
